title: FeatureMAP Tutorial
section: FeatureMAP: A Feature-based Metabolite Functional Module Identification and Annotation Pipeline
text:
FeatureMAP: A Feature-based Metabolite Functional Module Identification and Annotation Pipeline
FeatureMAP (featuremap) is a feature-centric framework for untargeted metabolomics that identifies biologically meaningful metabolic modules directly from metabolomic data, rather than relying only on predefined pathways or fully confirmed metabolite identities. It is developed by the Shen Lab at Nanyang Technological University, Singapore.
The package provides a five-step workflow:

Data preparation: prepare a valid feature table and optional MS2 annotation table for FeatureMAP.
Feature annotation: annotate raw LC-MS features to metabolite candidates using MS1 (and optional MS2) information.
Subnetwork extraction: construct a robust prize-collecting Steiner forest (PCSF)-based metabolic subnetwork.
Module identification: detect functional modules by community detection and evaluate module significance.
Module annotation: interpret significant modules with database knowledge, optional PubMed evidence, and LLM reasoning, either in a fast two-call mode or in an advanced multi-agent debate mode that can also synthesize the annotated modules into one study-level picture.

This workflow helps convert feature-level metabolomics signals into interpretable biological modules in a reproducible and analysis-ready format.

title: FeatureMAP Tutorial
text:
Aim of This Tutorial
This guide walks you through the two faces of FeatureMAP: the R package for command-line (code-based) workflow and the Shiny App/Web version for point-and-click exploration. In the end, you will be able to:

Prepare a valid feature table for FeatureMAP.
Run the complete five-step FeatureMAP workflow with R code.
Complete the same analysis with the FeatureMAP Shiny App/Web interface.
Understand and inspect key result objects and module-level interpretations.
Export interactive HTML reports for the module debate traces and the cross-module synthesis network.

Whether you favour the command line or a browser, this tutorial gives you everything you need to apply FeatureMAP confidently in your metabolomics projects.

title: 2  Data Preparation
text:
2.1 Input Data Format Requirements
This chapter describes how to prepare input data for the FeatureMAP pipeline. Unlike traditional workflows, FeatureMAP starts from feature-level metabolomics data.

title: 2  Data Preparation
text:
2.1.1 Required feature_table
FeatureMAP requires a data frame named feature_table with the following columns:








Column
Type
Description




variable_id
character
Unique feature ID (no duplicates)


mz
numeric
Feature m/z


rt
numeric
Retention time


polarity
character
Ion mode, must be "positive" or "negative"


mean_intensity
numeric
Mean intensity of the feature


condition
numeric
Numeric value representing the direction and magnitude of association for each feature, such as a log fold change, regression coefficient, or correlation coefficient


pvalue
numeric
Statistical p-value corresponding to the association measure in condition, used to reflect the strength of evidence









Note



condition captures the effect direction and size, while pvalue reflects its statistical significance. Together, they are used downstream to prioritize features before PCSF subnetwork extraction. In Subnetwork Extraction, FeatureMAP combines the two into a single feature importance score.








Tip



Positive- and negative-mode features can be analysed together in one table: keep the feature IDs unique across modes and set polarity accordingly.




2.1.2 Optional ms2_table
You can optionally provide an MS2 annotation table to improve feature-to-metabolite mapping confidence. MS2-based metabolite annotations can be obtained using the tidymass ecosystem.
Expected columns:

variable_id (character, unique)
HMDB.ID and/or KEGG.ID (character, can contain NA)

The MS2 table is used as auxiliary evidence only: a feature–metabolite pair generated by MS1 matching is flagged as MS2-supported when variable_id + HMDB.ID or variable_id + KEGG.ID also appears in the MS2 table. HMDB.ID is used first, and KEGG.ID serves as a fallback. MS2 rows that do not match any MS1 candidate do not create new annotations.
If ms2_table = NULL, FeatureMAP will proceed with MS1-based annotation only.

title: 3  Feature Annotation
text:
3.1 What annotate_feature() Does
This chapter describes Step 2 of the FeatureMAP pipeline: feature-level metabolite annotation using annotate_feature().
annotate_feature() performs feature-to-metabolite candidate annotation for LC–MS data and resolves the many-to-many relationship between features and metabolites. The procedure consists of below main stages:
The function returns a featuremap_result object with stage marker "feature_annotated", which is required for all downstream analyses.

title: 3  Feature Annotation
text:
MS1 database matching: Each LC–MS feature is matched to the FeatureMAP reference compound database using accurate mass and common ion forms. Only candidates carrying an HMDB or KEGG identifier are retained.
Metabolite Feature Cluster (MFC) construction: Features annotated to the same metabolite are grouped into MFCs based on retention-time proximity and ion relationships (e.g., adducts or isotopes).
Evidence-based scoring of MFCs: Each cluster is scored based on supporting evidence: user-supplied MS2 confirmation contributes the most (+150), canonical adducts ((M+H)+ in positive mode, (M-H)- in negative mode) contribute +50, and observed isotopic peaks or secondary adducts add smaller increments (+20/+10).
Iterative refinement of annotations: Conflicting annotations are resolved iteratively by removing low-confidence clusters and ambiguous feature assignments until convergence.








Note



One merged reference namespace. Earlier versions of FeatureMAP asked you to choose between a KEGG and an HMDB namespace with a refdata argument. This is no longer needed: annotate_feature() now matches against a merged HMDB + KEGG compound database (featuremap_compound), keeps both HMDB.ID and KEGG.ID for every candidate, and sets res$refdata to "all" automatically. All downstream steps work at the structure (InChI) level, so they are independent of the original identifier namespace.

3.4 Optional: Integrate Your Own MS2 Annotation
If you already have an MS2 annotation table, pass it to ms2_table:

ms2_table <- read.csv("your_ms2_annotation.csv")

  ms2_table = ms2_table,

title: 4  Subnetwork Extraction
text:
4.1 What extract_subnetwork() Does
This chapter describes Step 3 of the FeatureMAP pipeline: extracting a robust metabolic subnetwork with extract_subnetwork() using the prize-collecting Steiner forest (PCSF) strategy.
extract_subnetwork() integrates the refined feature annotations from Step 2 with a metabolic reaction network (MRN) and applies repeated PCSF optimization to identify a robust subnetwork.
At a high level, this step does the following:
This step moves the analysis from individual annotated features to a network-supported metabolite subnetwork, which is then used in downstream module extraction and interpretation.

title: 4  Subnetwork Extraction
text:
Compute feature importance: Feature-level statistical evidence is summarized from condition and pvalue. Both are min–max rescaled and combined as importance = sqrt(score_fc * score_p), and the result is written back into res$feature_table.
Build feature–metabolite mappings: The refined annotation table is projected onto MRN metabolite nodes, using HMDB.ID first and KEGG.ID as fallback, so that observed LC–MS features become terminal nodes attached to candidate metabolites.
Run repeated PCSF optimization: PCSF is run times times with relative Gaussian perturbation of the edge costs, so that the result does not depend on a single optimization run.
Aggregate robust network components: Node and edge frequencies are recorded across repeated runs, and the final subnetwork is constructed as the union of recurrent PCSF solutions.
Refine annotation using network support: Feature–metabolite mappings are updated based on network evidence, producing anno_feature_table2.

text:
4.3 Basic Usage

# res is the output from Step 2 (annotate_feature)
res <- extract_subnetwork(
  res = res,
  feature = "all",
  mrn = NULL,
  workers = 4,
  times = 100,
  b = 20,
  mu = 1e-4,
  w = 25,
  r = 0.20,
  grid_tune = FALSE
)







Tip



Use feature = "all" when you want the network to see the full statistical landscape, and feature = "sig" together with pcutoff when you prefer to seed the network only with significantly changed features.

4.5.1 Extracted PCSF subnetwork
The extracted metabolic subnetwork is stored as an igraph object, where metabolite nodes are named by their InChI string and feature nodes by their variable_id:

res$pcsf_subnet
# IGRAPH ... UNWB 2217 4949 --
# + attr: name (v/c), prize (v/n), type (v/c), freq (e/n), weight (e/n)
# + edges from ... (vertex names):
# + ... omitted several edges

Node attribute type is "Terminal" for LC–MS feature nodes and "Steiner" for metabolite nodes; prize stores the node appearance frequency, and edge attributes freq / weight store how often each edge was recovered across the repeated runs. In res$node_frequency, the type column instead distinguishes "feature" from "metabolite" nodes.

title: 5  Module Identification
text:
5.1 What identify_module() Does
This chapter describes Step 4 of the FeatureMAP pipeline: identifying functional modules from the PCSF-derived subnetwork using identify_module().
identify_module() performs community detection on the extracted subnetwork and then evaluates module significance using permutation testing.
At a high level, this step performs the following operations:
This step converts the extracted metabolic network into functional modules supported by both network topology and feature-level statistical evidence.

title: 5  Module Identification
text:
Construct a module detection graph: A metabolite-only subgraph is derived from the PCSF subnetwork. Metabolite nodes with low occurrence frequency across repeated PCSF runs are filtered out using node_freq. Nodes directly linked to observed features are labelled annotated; the remaining ones are labelled hidden.
Adjust edge weights: Edge weights are taken from the PCSF edge frequency and divided by the square root of the product of the two endpoint degrees in the full MRN, so that highly connected hub metabolites do not dominate the partition.
Detect network communities: One of four community detection algorithms partitions the network into candidate modules, which are then relabelled as compact IDs "M1", "M2", …
Prune module boundaries: Within each module, non-annotated terminal nodes are iteratively removed. Nodes dropped this way are kept in the table but flagged with Use_for_annotation = FALSE, so they no longer influence Step 5.
Compute module activity scores: Module scores summarize the statistical signal from features mapped to metabolites within the module.
Assess statistical significance: A permutation procedure with a gamma null model estimates empirical significance and controls the false discovery rate.

title: 5  Module Identification
text:
5.4 Clustering Methods

louvain
A fast modularity optimization algorithm that iteratively merges nodes and communities to maximize network modularity. It is widely used for large biological networks.
leading_eigen
A spectral method that partitions the network based on the leading eigenvectors of the modularity matrix. It identifies communities by separating nodes according to their contribution to modularity.
fast_greedy
An agglomerative hierarchical clustering method that starts with each node as its own community and progressively merges communities to increase modularity.
walktrap
A random-walk-based community detection algorithm that simulates short random walks on the network. The intuition is that random walks tend to remain within densely connected regions.

Different algorithms may produce slightly different module boundaries. Comparing multiple methods can help evaluate module robustness.

Each row represents a metabolite node belonging to an identified module:







Column
Description




Module
Module identifier ("M1", "M2", …)


INCHI_ID
InChI of the metabolite node, used as the primary key of the network


HMDB_ID, KEGG_ID, Compound_name
Metabolite identity carried over from the MRN


Node_freq
Frequency of the node across repeated PCSF runs (robustness)


Type
"annotated" if linked to an observed feature, "hidden" otherwise


Importance
Feature-derived importance, averaged with weighted_anno_score as weights


Use_for_annotation
FALSE for non-annotated terminal nodes pruned from the module boundary; those nodes are excluded from Step 5



Nodes with higher Node_freq and Importance values tend to represent more stable and feature-supported metabolites within the network.






Note



Here, annotated metabolites are nodes directly linked to observed LC–MS features through the feature annotation step, whereas hidden metabolites are Steiner nodes introduced during PCSF optimization to connect annotated metabolites within the metabolic reaction network. Hidden metabolites are not directly supported by measured features, but may provide important network context.




5.5.2 Module significance table
module_score summarizes statistics for each detected module:

head(res$module_score)
#   Module Module_size Annotated_nodes Module_score          p       fdr
# 1     M4          73              60    0.3278375 0.01174675 0.4463765
# 2    M12          51              44    0.2184320 0.08448563 0.6701799
# 3    M11          17              16    0.2090107 0.09908058 0.6701799
# 4     M3         123             113    0.1998797 0.11538420 0.6701799
# 5    M13          25              24    0.1797426 0.16015150 0.6701799
# 6    M17          32              31    0.1753071 0.17186291 0.6701799

sum(res$module_score$p < 0.05, na.rm = TRUE)
sum(res$module_score$fdr < 0.05, na.rm = TRUE)
# [1] 1
# [1] 0

Important columns include:

Module – module identifier, matching module_table
Module_size – number of metabolite nodes in the module
Annotated_nodes – number of nodes supported by feature annotations
Module_score – aggregated activity score of the module
p – permutation-based p-value
fdr – multiple-testing corrected p-value

Modules with lower p or fdr values indicate stronger statistical support and are typically prioritized for downstream biological interpretation.






Tip



If too many tiny modules appear, increase min_size or tighten node_freq. If modules are too coarse, try alternative methods, or lower louvain_resolution for broader and raise it for finer communities.

title: 6  Function Annotation
text:
6.1 What annotate_module() Does
This chapter describes Step 5 of the FeatureMAP pipeline: annotating statistically supported modules with annotate_module(), and, optionally, integrating the annotated modules into a study-level picture with synthesize_modules().
annotate_module() performs module-level biological interpretation for the modules that passed the significance filter in Step 4.
Regardless of the mode you choose, the function always starts from the same deterministic evidence, computed in R rather than by the language model:
The interpretation itself is then produced by an LLM, in one of two modes.

title: 6  Function Annotation
text:
Metabolite annotation: Metabolites of each significant module are annotated with class and pathway metadata from both HMDB and KEGG references.
Top and anchor metabolite selection: Module members are ranked by 0.7 * Importance + 0.3 * Node_freq, and a Gaussian mixture model selects the leading metabolites that represent the module.
Module-level statistics: Signal concentration, KEGG and HMDB pathway coverage, global direction of change, and the endogenous/exogenous origin profile are computed.



6.1.1 Fast mode (mode = "fast")
A two-call pipeline, and the recommended default:

LLM call 1 – from metabolite evidence only (no phenotype), the model returns hypothesis_type, title and functional_summary.
Optional PubMed retrieval – the module title and each top metabolite are searched separately; the retained articles are deduplicated by PMID.
LLM call 2 – with the study context and the literature, the model returns phenotype_relationship, confidence_label and rationale.



6.1.2 Advanced mode (mode = "advanced")
A multi-agent debate pipeline that produces one row per surviving hypothesis instead of one row per module:

P0 Proposer – generates 1–3 candidate biochemical hypotheses from the metabolite evidence only.
S1 Skeptic – challenges each hypothesis on biochemical, origin, species and biospecimen grounds, without seeing the phenotype or the literature.
P1 Proposer revision – keeps, modifies or drops each hypothesis.
S2 / P2 – a second debate round runs only if revisions were made or major challenges remained unanswered.
Optional PubMed – anchor-metabolite and per-hypothesis title searches, retained for the arbiter only.
A0 Arbiter – delivers a final accepted / rejected verdict per hypothesis, with a confidence score and a residual-ambiguity note.
Optional synthesis – with synthesize = TRUE, accepted hypotheses from all modules are integrated across modules (see Section 6.6).







Tip



Use fast mode for routine analyses and for a first look at your data: it is markedly cheaper and faster. Use advanced mode when a module is ambiguous, when you want to see the reasoning that supports or rejects an interpretation, or when you want a study-level synthesis across modules.

After successful annotation:

res_fast$stage

# [1] "module_function"     "module_evidence"     "study_context"

# [7] "anno_feature_table2" "anno_feature_table1" "feature_table"

6.4.1 Module interpretation table
module_function contains the final module-level interpretation. In fast mode it has one row per annotated module; in advanced mode one row per accepted hypothesis (or a single summary row when all hypotheses of a module were rejected).

res_fast$module_function$title
# Example output; LLM-generated text depends on the model and prompt.
# [1] "Purine nucleotide turnover and energy metabolism"

res_fast$module_function %>%
  dplyr::select(module_id, hypothesis_type, title, confidence_label) %>%
  as.data.frame()

# 1        M4 Host-Endogenous Purine nucleotide turnover and energy metabolism           medium

res_fast$module_function$functional_summary[1]
# [1] "This module is enriched for purine-related metabolites and connected cofactors, suggesting altered nucleotide turnover and cellular energy metabolism."

res_fast$module_function$phenotype_relationship[1]
# [1] "In the provided plasma phenotype context, the module may reflect changes in systemic purine metabolism; interpret this together with the module statistics and literature evidence."








Column
Description

annotation_mode
"fast" or "advanced"

  as.data.frame() %>%
  left_join(res_fast$module_score, by = c("module_id" = "Module")) -> module_report

write.csv(module_report, "module_function_report.csv", row.names = FALSE)

All evidence used for the annotation is kept in res$module_evidence:

names(res_fast$module_evidence)
# [1] "class_coverage" "pathway_coverage" "pubmed_evidence" "top_metabolites"

text:
6.5 Interactive HTML Reports

6.5.1 Debate traces
With debate_html = TRUE, advanced mode writes one chat-style page per module to html_dir, named debate_<module_id>.html. You can also re-export them later from a saved result, without calling the LLM again:

# all modules
export_debate_html(res = res_adv, html_dir = "featuremap_html")

# a single module
export_debate_html(res = res_adv, module_id = "M1", html_dir = "featuremap_html")

Each page shows the Proposer, Skeptic and Arbiter turns in order, so you can follow exactly why a hypothesis was kept, revised or rejected.


6.5.2 Synthesis network
When synthesize = TRUE, an interactive network page synthesis_network.html is written to html_dir automatically. To re-export it from a saved result:

export_synthesis_network_html(
  res         = res_adv,
  html_dir    = "featuremap_html",
  output_file = "synthesis_network.html"
)

generate_synthesis_network_html() does the same from a bare res$module_synthesis list, which is useful when you keep only the synthesis object:

generate_synthesis_network_html(
  synthesis     = res_adv$module_synthesis,
  study_context = res_adv$study_context,
  output_dir    = "featuremap_html",
  output_file   = "synthesis_network.html"
)

title: 6  Function Annotation
text:
6.6 Cross-Module Synthesis
synthesize_modules() takes the accepted hypotheses of all annotated modules and integrates them into one picture of the study. It is run automatically by annotate_module(mode = "advanced", synthesize = TRUE), and can also be called on its own, for example to re-run the synthesis with a stronger model:

res_adv <- synthesize_modules(
  res           = res_adv,
  study_context = list(
    species     = "human",
    biospecimen = "plasma",
    phenotype   = "your disease phenotype"
  ),
  provider    = "openai",
  llm_model   = "gpt-4.1",
  llm_api_key = Sys.getenv("OPENAI_API_KEY"),
  max_tokens  = 4000,
  temperature = 0
)







Important



synthesize_modules() requires advanced mode output. Fast mode produces one flat annotation per module and no hypothesis-level verdicts, so it cannot be synthesized this way. If study_context is NULL, it is taken from res$study_context.
If only one module has accepted hypotheses, the LLM call is skipped and res$module_synthesis is returned with the deterministic parts only.


The synthesis combines two very different kinds of links:

Biology links are proposed by the LLM from hypothesis titles and summaries only, and are deliberately sparse.
Biochemical links are computed in R from direct MRN edges between top metabolites and from pathway ID overlap, so they are fully deterministic.

Results are stored in res$module_synthesis:

names(res_adv$module_synthesis)
# [1] "nodes" "clusters" "biology_links" "biochemical_links"
#     "relationships_sparse" "relationships" "module_relationships"
#     "summary" "raw_response"

res_adv$module_synthesis$clusters
# Example output; synthesis is generated from accepted advanced-mode hypotheses.
# # A tibble: 1 x 3
#   cluster_id cluster_theme                     node_ids
#   <chr>      <chr>                             <list>
# 1 C1         Purine and energy metabolism      <chr [1]>

res_adv$module_synthesis$module_relationships
# # A tibble: 1 x 5
#   module_a module_b relation_type n_biochemical_links n_biology_links
#   <chr>    <chr>    <chr>                       <int>           <int>
# 1 M4       M12      biochemical                     2               0

cat(res_adv$module_synthesis$summary)
# The accepted module hypotheses form a study-level pattern centered on purine
# metabolism and related energy-transfer chemistry. The biochemical links should
# be interpreted together with the original module scores and phenotype context.


nodes – one row per accepted hypothesis, with node_id ("<module_id>::<hypothesis_id>") and its assigned cluster
clusters – thematic clusters (cluster_id, cluster_theme, member node_ids)
biology_links / relationships_sparse – LLM-proposed cross-module relationships with rationales
biochemical_links – MRN-edge and pathway-overlap evidence between hypotheses
relationships – the merged relationship table used to draw the network
module_relationships – module-pair summary, with relation_type being biochemical, biology, both or none
summary – the narrative integrating clusters, cross-module links and the phenotype
raw_response – the original LLM response, kept for transparency

title: 6  Function Annotation
text:
6.7 Practical Checks Before Running

head(res$module_score)
sum(res$module_score$fdr < 0.05, na.rm = TRUE)
sum(res$module_score$p < 0.05, na.rm = TRUE)

If no module passes your threshold, annotate_module() returns an empty module_function and warns you. Either relax the filter (p = "p" instead of "fdr") or revisit Step 4 before trying module annotation.

title: 6  Function Annotation
text:
6.8 Common Issues

No module annotated. Nothing passed p/pcutoff. Switch to p = "p", raise pcutoff, or revisit the module identification settings.
PubMed retrieval is slow. Start with a shorter years window, fewer significant modules, or pubmed = FALSE while you validate the workflow.
Advanced mode is expensive. Each module costs several LLM calls. Validate the pipeline in fast mode first, then re-run the modules you care about in advanced mode.
synthesize = TRUE was ignored. Synthesis only runs in advanced mode; in fast mode a warning is emitted and the step is skipped.
Provider/model mismatch. Make sure llm_model exists for the selected provider, and remember that provider = "local" requires a non-empty base_url.

title: 6  Function Annotation
text:
6.9 Next Step
Module annotation is the last step of the R-package workflow. res$module_function, res$module_evidence and res$module_synthesis, together with the exported HTML pages, contain everything you need for downstream reporting.
If you want to continue with the interactive interface, move to Shiny App Installation to start the Shiny tutorial.

7.3 Accounts and Sign In
The app has an optional account layer:

Uploads are capped at 500 MB per file by default, which is enough for most feature tables and for a custom reference database. If you need a larger limit for a local run, set it before launching the app:

you can keep the built-in reference resources or upload your own

The app accepts .csv, .rda and .RData files, up to 500 MB per file by default.






Important



Choosing between an HMDB and a KEGG namespace is no longer needed. FeatureMAP now uses one built-in merged database that keeps both HMDB and KEGG identifiers, exactly as described in R package-Feature Annotation.



8.4.1 Reference Source

Default reference (recommended): use the MS1 annotation database and the metabolic reaction network that ship with the app.
Upload reference datasets: two extra upload fields appear, for your own MS1 Annotation Database (.rda, a metid-compatible database whose spectra.info contains Lab.ID, Compound.name, Formula, HMDB.ID, KEGG.ID, CAS.ID, mz, RT and Submitter) and your own Metabolic Reaction Network (.rda, an igraph object). Format examples can be downloaded from featuremap_resources.

For detailed column definitions of feature_table and ms2_table, see R package-Data Preparation.

title: 8  Data Upload
text:
8.5 Recommended: Start with Demo Data
For most users, the best way to learn the app is to start with the built-in demo data.
The recommended sequence is:

click Use Demo Data – the two upload fields are filled with demo_feature_table.rda and demo_ms2.rda
keep Default reference (recommended)
click Load
confirm that the preview tables and the success message appear on the right






This lets you move through the full Shiny workflow first, before switching to your own dataset.






Tip



Use Demo Data only stages the demo files; you still need to click Load to place them into the current session. Download Demo saves the same two tables as a zip file, which is handy as a template for formatting your own data.

title: 8  Data Upload
text:
8.6 Next Step
Once the data are loaded successfully, the Next Step button becomes available. Click it to continue to Feature Annotation.

9.1 Enter the Feature Annotation Page
This chapter focuses on how to use Step 2: Feature Annotation in FeatureMAP Shiny. The detailed method, parameter definitions, and output structure have already been introduced in R package-Feature Annotation, so here we focus on the app workflow itself.
After finishing Data Upload, click Next Step, or open Analysis → 2 Feature Annotation in the navigation bar.
The purpose of this step is to map metabolomics features to candidate metabolites and prepare the refined annotation table for downstream network analysis.

title: 9  Feature Annotation
text:
9.3 Run Feature Annotation
Once the parameters are ready, click Run.
A progress card appears while the step is running. When it finishes, the card reports:

Annotated features – how many of the uploaded features received at least one candidate, with the percentage
Feature-metabolite pairs – how many annotation rows were produced

The result panel on the right is updated automatically and the Next Step button becomes available.
If you did not provide an MS2 annotation table in the previous step, the app will still run using MS1-based annotation only.

title: 9  Feature Annotation
text:
9.4 Result Area

9.4.1 Summary
The Summary tab reports how much annotation ambiguity was removed by the refinement stage, comparing the state before and after filtering along two axes:

Candidate metabolites per feature – how many metabolites a single feature is still assigned to
Feature groups per metabolite – how many metabolite feature clusters (MFCs) point at the same metabolite






This view is useful for checking whether the annotation step completed normally and whether the refinement reduced redundancy.


9.4.2 Annotation Table
The Annotation Table tab contains the detailed feature-to-metabolite annotation results produced by this step; it is the same table as res$anno_feature_table1 in the R package.





For a full explanation of the result columns, see R package-Feature Annotation. The table supports searching, sorting, and column filtering directly in the browser.

title: 9  Feature Annotation
section: 9.5 Recommended: Run the Demo Data First
text:
9.5 Recommended: Run the Demo Data First
If you followed the previous chapter and loaded the built-in demo data, the recommended workflow here is:

keep the default parameter settings
click Run
wait for the annotation step to finish
check the Summary tab first
then open Annotation Table to inspect the detailed annotation results

This is the easiest way to understand what the step produces before applying it to your own dataset.






Tip



If the result table looks empty, first check whether Data Upload finished successfully in the previous step, and then confirm that the input files were loaded correctly.

Once feature annotation is complete, click Next Step to continue to PCSF Subnetwork.

After finishing Feature Annotation, click Next Step, or open Analysis → 3 PCSF Subnetwork in the navigation bar.
The purpose of this step is to use the PCSF strategy to extract a network-supported metabolite subnetwork for downstream module identification.

title: 10  Subnetwork Extraction

10.3 Run PCSF Subnetwork Extraction
Once the parameters are ready, click Run PCSF.
The app shows a progress card while the repeated PCSF runs are executed. When the step finishes successfully, the result panel on the right is updated automatically and the Next Step button becomes available.
If you enable grid tuning, the selected best b / w combination is recorded and shown later in the Analysis Parameters card on the Results Download page.

title: 10  Subnetwork Extraction
text:
10.4 Result Area

10.4.1 Subnetwork
The Subnetwork tab shows the extracted PCSF network, provided Visualize PCSF subnetwork was enabled in the parameter area. If visualization is disabled, the run still finishes normally, but this tab stays empty.





The network is interactive: you can zoom, drag and click nodes. Two selectors above the plot help you navigate a large network:

the Feature selector highlights a chosen LC–MS feature and its directly connected metabolites
the Metabolite selector highlights a chosen metabolite and its directly connected features

The rows listed under the network follow the current selection. The legend distinguishes Feature nodes (orange) from Metabolite nodes (blue).


10.4.2 Annotation Table 2
The Annotation Table 2 tab contains the network-refined annotation results generated after PCSF extraction, that is res$anno_feature_table2 in the R package. Compared with the previous annotation table, it adds the network evidence (edge_freq, weighted_anno_score, confidence_rank) and is the main output carried into the next step.





For a full explanation of the result columns, see R package-Subnetwork Extraction.

title: 10  Subnetwork Extraction
section: 10.5 Recommended: Run the Demo Data First
text:
10.5 Recommended: Run the Demo Data First
If you followed the previous chapters and loaded the built-in demo data, the recommended workflow here is:

keep the default parameter settings
leave Enable grid tuning unchecked for the first run
keep Visualize PCSF subnetwork enabled if you want to see the network directly
click Run PCSF
check the Subnetwork tab first
then open Annotation Table 2 to inspect the refined results

This is the easiest way to understand what the PCSF step produces before tuning parameters on your own dataset.






Tip



If the result tab stays empty, first check whether Feature Annotation finished successfully in the previous step. Note that repeated PCSF runs are the slowest part of the workflow: lowering Iterations (final) gives a quicker first look, at the cost of robustness.

10.6 Next Step
Once subnetwork extraction is complete, click Next Step to continue to Module Identification.

After finishing Subnetwork Extraction, click Next Step, or open Analysis → 4 Module Identification in the navigation bar.
The purpose of this step is to identify functional modules from the extracted PCSF subnetwork.

11.3 Run Module Identification
Once the parameters are ready, click Run.
Module detection is followed by the permutation test, so this step takes a while with the default 100 permutations. When it finishes, the result panel is updated automatically and the Next Step button becomes available.

title: 11  Module Identification
text:
11.4 Result Area

11.4.1 Visualization
The Visualization tab shows one detected module at a time as a network.





Two selectors sit above the plot:

the Module selector chooses which module (M1, M2, …) to display
the Metabolite selector highlights one metabolite and its directly connected neighbours inside that module

The legend distinguishes Annotated metabolites (green), which are linked to observed LC–MS features, from Hidden metabolites (red), which are Steiner nodes added during PCSF optimization to keep the module connected.


11.4.2 Module Score
The Module Score tab shows the quantitative summary for every detected module: size, number of annotated nodes, module score, permutation p-value and FDR. This table tells you which modules are worth interpreting in the next step.







11.4.3 Module Table
The Module Table tab shows the detailed module membership: which metabolite belongs to which module, its HMDB and KEGG identifiers, node frequency, type and importance.





For a full explanation of the columns in both tables, see R package-Module Identification.

title: 11  Module Identification
section: 11.5 Recommended: Run the Demo Data First
text:
11.5 Recommended: Run the Demo Data First
If you followed the previous chapters and loaded the built-in demo data, the recommended workflow here is:

keep the default parameter settings
click Run
wait for module identification and the permutation test to finish
open Visualization first to inspect the detected modules
then review Module Score to see which modules are significant
finally check Module Table for the detailed module membership results

This is the easiest way to understand what this step produces before tuning parameters on your own dataset.






Tip



If no module appears, first check whether Subnetwork Extraction finished successfully and whether the extracted subnetwork contains enough structure for community detection. Lowering Minimum module size or the Node frequency threshold keeps more of the network in play.

11.6 Next Step
Once module identification is complete, click Next Step to continue to Function Interpretation.

title: 12  Function Interpretation

After finishing Module Identification, click Next Step, or open Analysis → 5 Function Interpretation in the navigation bar.
The purpose of this step is to turn statistically supported modules into interpretable biology, using the module’s own metabolite evidence, optional PubMed literature, and a large language model.

title: 12  Function Interpretation
text:
12.3 Fast Mode and Advanced Mode
The Annotation Mode switch chooses between the two pipelines described in R package-Function Annotation:

Fast – a two-call pipeline producing one interpretation per module. This is the cheaper and faster option, and the right one for a first pass.
Advanced – a multi-agent debate: a Proposer drafts 1–3 candidate hypotheses, a Skeptic challenges them over up to two rounds, and an Arbiter accepts or rejects each one.







Tip



In the app, Advanced mode is not a set of separate options: the per-module debate transcript and the cross-module synthesis are always produced as part of an Advanced run, and appear as their own result tabs.

title: 12  Function Interpretation
text:
12.4 Run Function Interpretation
Once the parameters are ready, click Run.
The app calls the model module by module, so this step is the slowest one and its runtime grows with the number of significant modules, with Advanced mode, and with PubMed enabled. If no module passes the selected cutoff, the run finishes normally and the result panel reports that nothing passed.






Note



API keys are entered per session and are used only for the current run; they are not stored in your results.

title: 12  Function Interpretation
text:
12.5 Result Area (Fast Mode)
In Fast mode the right panel shows one module at a time, chosen with the module selector in the toolbar.





Each report opens with the module title and a row of pills – module ID, hypothesis type, and confidence – followed by five sections:







Section
Content




Function Interpretation
The functional summary, plus the core driver (anchor) metabolites behind it


Biochemical Context
Chemical-class profile, KEGG and HMDB pathway coverage, and the endogenous/exogenous origin profile


Module Statistics
The supporting metabolites of the module and the global direction of change


Phenotype & Literature
The phenotype relationship, plus clickable PMID links when PubMed was enabled


Evidence Strength
The confidence label and the rationale behind it

title: 12  Function Interpretation
text:
12.6 Result Area (Advanced Mode)
In Advanced mode the right panel has three tabs.

12.6.1 Accepted Interpretations





The same report layout as Fast mode, but with two selectors: one for the module and one for the accepted hypothesis within that module. A module can therefore carry more than one accepted interpretation.


12.6.2 Debate History





An embedded chat-style transcript of the debate for the selected module, showing the Proposer, Skeptic and Arbiter turns in order. This is where you see why a hypothesis survived or was rejected. It is the same page that export_debate_html() writes in the R package.


12.6.3 Cross-Module Synthesis





An interactive network integrating the accepted hypotheses from all modules into thematic clusters, with links that are either proposed by the model from the hypothesis summaries or computed deterministically from metabolic-network edges and pathway overlap. It corresponds to res$module_synthesis and to export_synthesis_network_html() in the R package.
Both HTML reports can be exported on the Results Download page.

title: 12  Function Interpretation
section: 12.7 Recommended: Run the Demo Data First
text:
12.7 Recommended: Run the Demo Data First
If you followed the previous chapters and loaded the built-in demo data, the recommended workflow here is:

keep the default significance settings, or switch the metric to p-value if no module passes the FDR cutoff
fill in Study Context with the species, biospecimen and phenotype of your study
start in Fast mode, with Use PubMed literature off, so the first run is quick and cheap
provide the LLM provider, model ID and API key
click Run and review the generated title, summary, confidence and rationale
once the setup works, re-run the modules you care about in Advanced mode, with PubMed enabled







Tip



If this step returns no results, first check whether any module passed the cutoff in Module Identification. If the run fails immediately, check the model ID and the API key – an unknown model name for the selected provider is the most common cause.

title: 12  Function Interpretation
text:
12.8 Next Step
Once function interpretation is complete, click Results to download the generated tables, networks and reports.

title: 13  Results Download
text:
13.1 Enter the Results Page
This chapter focuses on how to use Step 6: Results Download in FeatureMAP Shiny. This page is the export center of the workflow, where you review the run, choose which outputs to keep, and download them as a single compressed archive.
After finishing Function Interpretation, click Results, or open Analysis → 6 Results Download in the navigation bar.

title: 13  Results Download
text:
13.2 Summary Cards
At the top of the work area, four cards summarize the current run:

Uploaded Features – the size of the input feature table
Annotated Features – how many features survived into the network-refined annotation table
Detected Modules – how many modules were found in Step 4
Annotated Modules – how many significant modules were interpreted, out of how many passed the cutoff, together with the metric and mode used (for example FDR < 0.05 (Advanced))

This is a quick way to check that the workflow ran as expected before exporting anything.

title: 13  Results Download
text:
13.3 Export Options
The left panel is where you choose what to export.





Tables – Annotation table 1, Annotation table 2, Module score, Module table, Module function. Everything that is ready is ticked for you, and the Table format selector offers Excel (.xlsx), CSV (one file per table) or RData.
Networks – the PCSF subnetwork and the module networks. When Module network is selected, an extra selector lets you export all modules or only the ones you choose. The Network format selector offers interactive HTML or GraphML for use in Cytoscape or igraph.
Reports – this section appears only after an Advanced mode run in Step 5, and offers the Debate transcripts and the Cross-module synthesis network as standalone HTML pages.





Items that are not ready yet, because the corresponding step has not been run, cannot be selected. Clicking Download packages everything you selected into one zip archive.

title: 13  Results Download
text:
13.4 Analysis Parameters
The right panel contains an Analysis Parameters card that records the settings used in the current run, one block per step:






Data & Reference – reference database used, feature table size, whether an MS2 table was provided
Feature Annotation – column type, MS1 and RT tolerance, isotope number, threads
Subnetwork (PCSF) – terminal selection and cutoff, fixed b / w or the best pair found by grid tuning
Module Identification – algorithm, node frequency threshold, minimum module size, permutations, seed
Function Interpretation – mode, significance cutoff, LLM provider and model

Steps that have not been run are shown as pending. This card is the record to keep alongside your exported files when you write up the analysis.

title: 13  Results Download
text:
13.5 Back to Home
The Back to Home button returns the app to the Home page after confirmation.





Before returning, the app clears the analysis results held in the current session, so you can start a new analysis from a clean state.






Note



This action clears the in-app analysis state only. It does not delete files that you have already downloaded to your own computer, so download what you need first.

title: 13  Results Download
text:
13.6 Recommended Export Workflow
For most users, the recommended workflow on this page is:

check the four summary cards at the top
confirm the result tables you want to keep and choose the table format
add the networks you want, and pick which modules to include
for an Advanced run, add the debate transcripts and the cross-module synthesis under Reports
review the Analysis Parameters card
click Download
click Back to Home when you are ready to start a new analysis

This gives you a clean, reproducible backup of the current run in one compressed file.
